originalTitle: He Had It Coming review – this messy crime-comedy has all the subtlety of a mallet to the crotch
summary: It’s sporadically very funny, but the tone of this blackly comic murder-mystery is all over the place. It want to tackle big issues, but seems afraid of its own politics
content: ‘But I can’t get an F,” wails Elise (Lydia West) in the first episode of the Australian campus comedy He Had It Coming, shoulders slumping like soufflés as her tutor peers pityingly at her terrible paintings. “I’m here on a scholarship? I’m here to be an artist?!” Alas, poor Elise. No amount of wounded upspeak can disguise the fact that she is an aspiring artist in much the same way a bag of flour is an aspiring pastry. Her “work”, bless it, consists of daubing clothes on to impressionist nudes – a “protest”, apparently, against the patriarchy and its preoccupation with “ancient bush”. Unctuous Professor Phoenix (Harry Greenwood) is unimpressed. “Hmm,” he sighs, pouting affectedly at Elise’s “feminist reimagining” of Manet’s Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe; the picnic’s enigmatic nude now sporting a pair of jeans and oversized novelty spectacles. Mon Dieu! The problem, explains Phoenix, slowly, is a lack of ambition. Feminist art isn’t for amateurs. “Be radical,” he smirks, as Elise quietly broils with rage. “Don’t settle for mediocrity.” The nerve! “These men are holding us back,” she roars later at new pal Barbara (Natasha Liu Bordizzo), a prickly fashion influencer who is being slut-shamed by the campus jocks for having tipsily humped a stranger’s thigh at a party. “Yes,” agrees Barbara. “Let’s go vandalise something!” And so to the quadrant, where, in the dead of night, a mallet is applied to the genitals of the statue of the university’s hopelessly male namesake. “FTP!” tee-hees Elise drunkenly. “That means Fuck The Patriarchy!” The next morning, however, brings trouble with a capital strewth. The body of an alpha-jock has been discovered, sans penis, at the foot of the malleted effigy. “Oh, that poor boy,” gasps Elise’s lovely mum. “And his doodle.” Others are less gracious. “Hell, yeah,” whoops a member of the university’s feminist collective. The victim was, it seems, a rapist and a bully. “He had it coming.” As, apparently, did the next victim – a men’s rights activist whose corpse has been similarly de-doodled. Who, we gasp, dunnit? He Had It Coming’s tagline is “Bad feminists. Worse detectives”, which makes it sound like an edgy Rosemary & Thyme reboot in which Pam Ferris and Felicity Kendal trample topsoil through a succession of crime scenes while shouting about Mooncups. But this Sydney-set series has loftier ambitions. What happens, it asks, when it is men, rather than women, who are forced to live with the constant threat of sexual intimidation and assault? Among the hot potatoes swept up in the ensuing eight episodes are misogyny, victim-blaming and social media’s complicity in harassment. And yet it quickly becomes clear that this black comedy is not entirely comfortable with the task it has set itself. It seems alarmed, somehow, by its own politics. Like poor Elise’s hopeless paintings, He Had It Coming appears to believe that simply pointing at something bad while going “nyer” is enough to convince onlookers that this constitutes a searing analysis of said bad thing. Which it most certainly does not. Instead, it spends most of its time avoiding the tricky stuff and focusing on its gleefully silly murder investigation, which entails Elise and Barbara galumphing around campus like pantomime horses while neighing quarter-witted theories into their neon-pink walkie-talkies. Consequently, the tone is all over the place. The second episode involves a man’s trousers falling down, a discussion about radical feminism, and a dog that can wink. All of which ensures that the bits that do attempt to make a serious point land with the finesse of a mallet to the genitals. Still, He Had It Coming is, sporadically, very funny. It’s also much too cartoonish to be in any way offensive. Instead, the series seems perpetually distracted by its own puppyish daftness, wagging its tail as it drags yet another mutilated corpse across the refectory floor. Here, everyone is an idiot. The women are as self-delusional and/or unpleasant as the men, and everyone, ultimately, is offered a chance at redemption. It’s a mess, but it’s an energetic mess and its heart – if not its doodle – is in the right place. Not an F, then. But a well-earned C. He Had It Coming aired on BBC Three and is available on iPlayer
chineseTitle: 《他来了》评论——这部混乱的犯罪喜剧充满了木槌敲击胯部的所有微妙之处
chineseSummary: 偶尔很有趣，但这种黑色喜剧谋杀之谜的基调无处不在。它想要解决重大问题，但似乎害怕自己的政治
chineseContent: 在澳大利亚校园喜剧《他来了》的第一集中，埃莉斯（莉迪亚·韦斯特饰）哀嚎道：“但我拿不到 F。”当她的导师怜悯地看着她糟糕的画作时，她的肩膀像舒芙蕾一样耷拉着。“我是靠奖学金来的？我是来当艺术家的？！”唉，可怜的伊莉丝。再多的受伤的夸奖也无法掩盖她是一位有抱负的艺术家的事实，就像一袋面粉是一块有抱负的糕点一样。天哪，她的“作品”包括在印象派裸体上涂抹衣服——显然是对父权制及其对“古老灌木丛”的关注的“抗议”。油腻的菲尼克斯教授（哈利·格林伍德饰）不为所动。 “嗯，”他叹了口气，对埃莉斯对马奈的《草地上的午餐》的“女权主义重新想象”做出了假撅嘴的表情。野餐中神秘的裸体现在穿着牛仔裤和超大的新奇眼镜。我的上帝！菲尼克斯慢慢地解释说，问题在于缺乏雄心。女权主义艺术不适合业余爱好者。 “要激进一点，”他傻笑着说，而埃莉斯则默默地怒火中烧。 “不要满足于平庸。”神经！ “这些男人拖了我们的后腿，”她后来对新朋友芭芭拉（娜塔莎·刘·博迪佐饰）咆哮道。芭芭拉是一位易怒的时尚影响者，因在聚会上醉酒地拱起陌生人的大腿而受到校园运动员的羞辱。 “是的，”芭芭拉同意。 “我们去破坏一些东西吧！”象限也是如此，在夜深人静的时候，有人用木槌敲击大学无可救药的同名男性雕像的生殖器。 “FTP！”埃莉斯喝醉了。 “这意味着去他妈的父权制！”然而，第二天早上，大量的资金就带来了麻烦。在木槌雕像的脚下发现了一具没有阴茎的阿尔法运动员的尸体。 “哦，那个可怜的男孩，”伊莉斯可爱的妈妈喘着气说。 “还有他的涂鸦。”其他人则不太感激
